1.title: Properties of Curved Spherical Mirrors
1.text:
Properties of Curved Spherical Mirrors

A spherical mirror is shaped like a section of a hollow sphere, with a center of curvature C and a radius of curvature r.

Our big question for this lesson: what are the advantages and disadvantages of curved mirrors compared to plane mirrors? Grab a shiny metal spoon and move it toward and away from your face. Look at both sides. Your image may grow, shrink, or even flip upside down! What you see depends on the mirror's shape and where the object is.

A spherical mirror is shaped as if it were cut from a hollow sphere. In Figure 10, the mirror, M, shares its geometric center, C, with a sphere of radius r. That distance r is called the radius of curvature.

The straight line through C and M is the principal axis. It's perpendicular to the mirror's surface and divides the mirror in half.

2.title: Your Investigation Toolkit
2.text:
Your Investigation Toolkit

Collect evidence in your Science Journal and investigate with activities.

Use your Science Journal to record the evidence you collect as you work through the readings and activities in this lesson.

Online, the Virtual Investigation called Ray Tracing for Mirrors lets you use a computer model to see how a curved mirror's properties change the way it reflects light. And the PhysicsLAB called Concave Mirror Images asks you to explain why different mirrors produce different images.

3.title: The Focal Point
3.text:
The Focal Point

The focal point is where incident rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflecting; the focal length is f equals r divided by 2.

Sunlight reaching Earth is almost perfectly parallel, because the Sun is so far away. Point a concave mirror's principal axis at the Sun, and all those reflected rays pass through one point. You can find it by moving a sheet of paper toward and away from the mirror until the sunlight shrinks to its smallest, sharpest spot.

That spot is the focal point, F: the point where incident rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflecting from the mirror. Look at the left mirror in Figure 10. The distance from M to F is exactly half the distance from M to C.

So the focal length, f, the distance between the mirror and the focal point, is f equals r divided by 2.

testIt.how: Slide the card along the axis of a mirror with r = 40 cm.

4.title: Concave Mirrors
4.text:
Concave Mirrors

A concave mirror curves inward, toward the observer, and has a positive focal length.

The inside of a spoon acts as a concave mirror. A concave mirror has an inwardly curving reflective surface whose edges curve toward the observer. Rays parallel to the principal axis reflect and meet at F. Because the rays really do converge there, the focal length of a concave mirror is positive.

The path also works in reverse. Rays that start at the focal point reflect off the mirror as parallel rays, as Figure 11 shows. That's how a flashlight works: put the bulb at the focal point, and out comes a tight, parallel beam. Car headlights and spotlights use concave mirrors the same way.

testIt.name: Bulb
testIt.how: Slide the bulb along the axis of a concave mirror with f = 10 cm.

5.title: Convex Mirrors
5.text:
Convex Mirrors

A convex mirror curves outward, away from the observer, with F and C behind the mirror.

Flip the spoon over. Its outer surface is a convex mirror, an outwardly curving reflective surface whose edges curve away from the observer, like the right side of Figure 10.

For a convex mirror, both the focal point and the center of curvature are behind the mirror. You see convex mirrors all the time: store security mirrors and many car side-view mirrors are convex.

6.title: Magnification
6.text:
Magnification

Magnification is m equals h sub i over h sub o, which equals negative x sub i over x sub o.

Another property of a curved mirror is magnification, m: the ratio of the image height to the object height. For a spherical mirror, m equals h sub i divided by h sub o, and that also equals negative x sub i divided by x sub o, the negative of the image position over the object position.

The sign of m tells you whether the image is upright or inverted. A positive m means upright, and a negative m means inverted. For virtual images, such as those from convex mirrors, x sub i is negative, so m is positive. Virtual images are always upright.

The size of m tells you about the image's size. If the absolute value of m is less than 1, the image is smaller than the object. If it's greater than 1, the image is larger.

testIt.name: Magnification
testIt.how: Move a 2.0 cm object in front of a concave mirror with f = 10 cm.

7.title: Ray Diagrams and Real Images
7.text:
Ray Diagrams and Real Images

A real image forms where reflected rays actually converge, so it can be projected on a screen.

Ray diagrams give you a picture of where a curved mirror forms an image. In Figure 12, rays from a banana reflect from a concave mirror and converge at point I. Converging rays form a real image, here inverted and larger than the object.

You can actually see a real image floating in space, if your eye is positioned so the rays forming it enter your eye. Face the wrong way and you see nothing. Put a sheet of paper or a movie screen at that point, and the image appears right on the screen. Virtual images can't be projected like this, since no rays really converge there.

How big is the real image? If the object is beyond C, the absolute value of the magnification is less than 1, so the image is smaller than the object. If the object is between C and F, the absolute value is greater than 1, so the image is larger.

testIt.name: Screen
testIt.how: Slide the screen in front of a mirror with f = 10 cm and an object at 30 cm.

8.title: Real Images with Concave Mirrors
8.text:
Real Images with Concave Mirrors

With the object beyond F, a concave mirror forms a real, inverted image: reduced beyond 2f, enlarged between f and 2f.

To keep ray diagrams simple, we use a one-dimensional object, an arrow, as in Figure 13. If the object position, x sub o, is greater than twice the focal length, the object is beyond the center of curvature, and the mirror makes a real, inverted image that's smaller than the object.

Move the object between C and the focal point, as on the right of Figure 13, and the image is still real and inverted, but now it's larger than the object. The color key helps you read the diagrams: the object is magenta, the image is lilac, and the light rays are red.

To find other points on the image, just repeat the trick: trace two rays from any point on the object, and where they cross after reflecting is that point's image.

9.title: Design a Mirror
9.text:
Design a Mirror

Systems can be designed to cause a desired effect, such as a large image.

Here's a cause-and-effect design puzzle. You want a mirror for shaving or applying makeup, so you want a large image. Should you use a plane, convex, or concave mirror?

Use the evidence from this lesson. A plane mirror gives a same-size image, and a convex mirror always shrinks the image. A concave mirror, with your face closer to it than its focal point, gives an upright, enlarged, virtual image. So a concave mirror is the winner. Try sketching your design, showing where your face should sit compared to F.

10.title: Problem-Solving Strategy, Ray Diagrams for Spherical Mirrors
10.text:
Problem-Solving Strategy, Ray Diagrams for Spherical Mirrors

Draw the principal axis, mirror, and object, then trace the parallel ray and the focus ray to find the image.

Here's a recipe for ray diagrams. First, on lined or graph paper, draw the principal axis as a horizontal line, leaving six blank lines above and six below. Second, mark the object, C, and F to scale. For a concave mirror with the object beyond C, put the mirror at the right and the object at the left. For a concave mirror with the object between C and F, put the mirror at the right, C in the center, and F halfway between. For anything else, put the mirror in the center, and the object or F, whichever is farther, at the left edge.

Third, draw the mirror as a vertical line 12 lines tall. This is the mirror's principal plane. Fourth, draw the object as an arrow and label its top O. For concave mirrors with objects inside C, keep it three lines high or less; otherwise make it six lines high. The vertical scale can differ from the horizontal one.

Fifth, draw ray 1, the parallel ray: it runs parallel to the principal axis, reflects off the principal plane, and passes through F. Sixth, draw ray 2, the focus ray: it passes through F, reflects off the principal plane, and leaves parallel to the axis. Seventh, if the reflected rays spread apart, extend dashed sight lines behind the mirror. Eighth, label the crossing point I, and draw the image as an arrow from the principal axis to I.

11.title: Virtual Images with Concave Mirrors
11.text:
Virtual Images with Concave Mirrors

An object between a concave mirror and its focal point gives a virtual, upright, enlarged image.

As an object moves toward F, its real image moves farther from the mirror. Right at the focal point, the reflected rays all leave parallel. They never meet, so we say the image is at infinity, and it can never be seen.

Move the object even closer, between the mirror and F, and something new happens. In Figure 14, ray 1 goes out parallel to the axis and reflects through F. Ray 2 travels along the line from F through the object point, then reflects parallel to the axis. These two reflected rays spread apart, so no real image forms. But their sight lines, extended behind the mirror, converge. A virtual image forms behind the mirror, upright and larger than the object.

How can you tell an image is virtual? The reflected rays diverge and only their sight lines meet, behind the mirror, so the image position is negative and the image can't be projected. In the photo, the nearby block tower looks upright and big, while objects farther away, beyond the focal point, appear upside down because the mirror forms real, inverted images of them.

testIt.name: Past F
testIt.how: Push the object toward the mirror (f = 10 cm).

12.title: Virtual Images with Convex Mirrors
12.text:
Virtual Images with Convex Mirrors

Convex mirrors form only virtual, upright, reduced images.

Rays reflected from a convex mirror always spread apart, so convex mirrors form only virtual images. Figure 15 shows two rays, though remember that countless rays leave the object.

Ray 1 approaches parallel to the principal axis and reflects as if it came from F, behind the mirror. Its sight line runs from where it hits the principal plane back through F. Ray 2 heads toward F behind the mirror and reflects parallel to the axis. The reflected rays diverge, but their sight lines meet behind the mirror. That's the image: virtual, upright, and smaller than the object.

testIt.name: Convex
testIt.how: Move an object in front of a convex mirror (f = −10 cm).

13.title: Field of View
13.text:
Field of View

By shrinking images, convex mirrors widen the field of view, the area an observer can see.

Smaller images might sound useless, but they're a big advantage. By shrinking images, convex mirrors let you see a larger area, called the field of view, and the image is visible from a wide range of angles.

That's why car passenger-side mirrors are convex, as in Figure 16. They shrink the driver's blind spot. The catch: smaller images make objects look farther away than they really are. So the warning printed on the mirror, objects may be closer than they appear, reminds drivers that a car in the mirror is nearer than it seems, which helps prevent accidents when changing lanes. That's one advantage and one disadvantage, right there in one mirror.

14.title: Spherical Aberration
14.text:
Spherical Aberration

Spherical aberration is the fuzziness caused when rays far from the principal axis do not converge at the focal point.

In ray diagrams, we drew the mirror as a straight vertical line. Real rays reflect off the curved mirror itself, as in Figure 17. Only parallel rays close to the principal axis reflect through the focal point. Rays farther out converge at points closer to the mirror. Because the rays don't all meet at one point, the image looks fuzzy. This defect is called spherical aberration.

A mirror ground into the shape of a parabola has no spherical aberration, because a parabola's shape sends every ray parallel to its axis through the same focal point. A sphere's shape only does this for rays near the axis. Big parabolic glass mirrors are expensive to make, so many telescopes use spherical mirrors along with smaller, specially designed secondary mirrors or lenses to correct the aberration.

Even famous telescopes face this problem. NASA launched the Hubble Space Telescope in 1990, expecting crisp images above the blurring atmosphere. Soon after, scientists discovered its main mirror had spherical aberration. In 1993, astronauts installed corrective optics called COSTAR, and for over twenty-five years Hubble sent back stunning images and enabled important discoveries.

15.title: The Mirror Equation
15.text:
The Mirror Equation

One over f equals one over x sub i plus one over x sub o.

Using the paraxial ray approximation, which says only rays close and nearly parallel to the principal axis form the image, together with the law of reflection, we get the mirror equation. It says the reciprocal of the focal length equals the sum of the reciprocals of the image position and the object position: one over f equals one over x sub i plus one over x sub o.

Signs matter. A virtual image has a negative image position, meaning it's behind the mirror. For concave mirrors, F is in front, so f is positive. For convex mirrors, F is behind, so f is negative.

The mirror equation is only approximate, because light from an object spreads out and not all of it stays near the axis. It works best when the mirror is small compared to its radius of curvature, since that keeps spherical aberration small.

16.title: Connecting Math to Physics, Adding and Subtracting Fractions
16.text:
Connecting Math to Physics, Adding and Subtracting Fractions

Solving the mirror equation: x sub i equals f times x sub o, divided by the quantity x sub o minus f.

To solve the mirror equation for one quantity, first move the fraction you want to the left side and everything else to the right. Start with one over f equals one over x sub i plus one over x sub o. Subtract to get one over x sub i equals one over f minus one over x sub o.

Next, combine the two fractions on the right using a common denominator, made by multiplying the denominators, f times x sub o. That gives one over x sub i equals the quantity x sub o minus f, all over f times x sub o. Flip both sides, and x sub i equals f times x sub o, divided by the quantity x sub o minus f.

The same steps give two more handy forms. The object position is x sub o equals f times x sub i, divided by the quantity x sub i minus f. And the focal length is f equals x sub i times x sub o, divided by the quantity x sub i plus x sub o.

17.title: Example Problem 2, Real Image Formation by a Concave Mirror
17.text:
Example Problem 2, Real Image Formation by a Concave Mirror

For an object beyond C, a concave mirror forms a real, inverted, reduced image.

A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 20.0 centimeters. You place a 2.0 centimeter tall object 30.0 centimeters from the mirror. What are the image position and image height?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the object and the mirror, then two principal rays to locate the image. Known: the object height is 2.0 centimeters, the object position is 30.0 centimeters, and the radius is 20.0 centimeters. Unknown: the image position and image height.

Step two: solve. The focal length is half the radius of curvature, so f equals 20.0 centimeters divided by 2, or 10.0 centimeters. Next, use x sub i equals f times x sub o, divided by the quantity x sub o minus f. That's 10.0 centimeters times 30.0 centimeters, divided by 30.0 centimeters minus 10.0 centimeters, which is 15.0 centimeters. It's a real image, in front of the mirror. For the height, the magnification equation gives h sub i equals negative x sub i times h sub o, divided by x sub o. That's negative 15.0 centimeters times 2.0 centimeters, divided by 30.0 centimeters, or negative 1.0 centimeter. The image is inverted and smaller.

Step three: evaluate. All positions and heights are in centimeters. A positive image position and a negative image height agree with the drawing: a real image, upside down.

18.title: Example Problem 3, Image in a Security Mirror
18.text:
Example Problem 3, Image in a Security Mirror

A convex mirror with a negative focal length forms a small, upright, virtual image.

A convex security mirror in a warehouse has a focal length of negative 0.50 meters. A 2.0 meter tall forklift is 5.0 meters from the mirror. What are the forklift's image position and image height?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the mirror and the forklift, plus two principal rays. Known: the object height is 2.0 meters, the object position is 5.0 meters, and f is negative 0.50 meters. Unknown: the image position and image height.

Step two: solve. Use x sub i equals f times x sub o, divided by the quantity x sub o minus f. That's negative 0.50 meters times 5.0 meters, divided by 5.0 meters minus negative 0.50 meters, which is negative 0.45 meters. It's a virtual image, behind the mirror. For the height, h sub i equals negative x sub i times h sub o, divided by x sub o: negative negative 0.45 meters times 2.0 meters, divided by 5.0 meters, which is 0.18 meters. The image is upright and smaller.

Step three: evaluate. All positions and heights are in meters. The negative position means a virtual image, and the positive height means upright. Both agree with the diagram. A whole forklift shrinks to 18 centimeters, which is why one mirror can show a whole aisle.

testIt.name: Forklift
testIt.how: Drive the 2.0 m forklift toward the convex mirror (f = −0.50 m).

19.title: Mirror Comparison
19.text:
Mirror Comparison

Plane and convex mirrors make only virtual images; concave mirrors make real or virtual images depending on the object position.

Table 1 sums up single mirrors with objects on the principal axis. A plane mirror has an infinite focal length. For any object, the image position is the negative of the object position, and the image is the same size and virtual.

A concave mirror has a positive focal length. With the object beyond r, the image falls between r and f, reduced, inverted, and real. With the object between r and f, the image lands beyond r, enlarged, inverted, and real. With the object between f and the mirror, the image position is negative, and the image is enlarged and virtual. A convex mirror has a negative focal length. For any object, the image is between the mirror and F, behind the mirror, with a negative position, reduced and virtual.

So here's the answer to our focus question. Plane mirrors give true-scale reflections but can't magnify or widen your view. Concave mirrors can focus light, project real images, and magnify objects inside their focal length, but they flip far objects and suffer spherical aberration. Convex mirrors widen your field of view, but they shrink images and make things look farther away than they are.
